<strong>Il y a quelques mois, dans les b: A few months ago, in La Converse’s offices, a first dialogue opened on the rise in violent crime among young Montrealers. Myriam Coppry, a coach who specializes in supporting immigrant parents, delivered this urgent message: “Very little room, or none at all, is left for parents when it comes to intervening with young people. (…) We can’t blame them once the harm is done, and then exclude them when it comes to solutions. That’s hypocrisy. We need to learn to hold them accountable without accusing them.”
<strong>En cette soirée d’hiver, sous la: On this winter evening, under the harsh ceiling lights of the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel, that is exactly what’s happening. Parents and children have come together to answer one question: how can they strengthen their bonds to prevent gun violence?
L’ambiance est étonnamment détendue, mai: The mood is surprisingly relaxed, but the ears are attentive. Facing about sixty parents and their teenagers, four community workers share their expertise. Among them are Hassan Benkhadra, father of three and coordinator at the Bureau associatif pour la diversité et la réinsertion in Saint-Léonard; Abdellah Azzouz, youth worker at the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel; Pierreson Vaval, longtime youth worker, father of four and director of the Coalition Pozé; and finally Kahina Bouchefa, clinical psychologist at the Hôpital du Sacré-Cœur-de-Montréal and mother of a teenage daughter.
Leur mission est claire : offrir aux fam: Their mission is clear: to give families tools to strengthen the bonds between parents and children, and so prevent a violence that hits racialized communities particularly hard.
Pierreson Vaval est le premier à prendre: Pierreson Vaval is the first to speak. “Violence is a symptom, a sign that something is wrong,” he begins in a steady voice. “We must not forget that our society reflects a negative image of who they are back to our racialized youth. This search for identity is so strong that they are sometimes ready to do anything to answer it: they’re ready to get hurt, to go to prison, as long as someone gives them an answer about who they are.”
La solution commence au sein de la famil: The solution starts within the family, he says: “We have to give our children an environment where they feel safe, physically, emotionally and psychologically.” Because, according to him, those who try to recruit young people and push them toward crime don’t hesitate to discredit their parents. “Your parents are out of their depth, they’re useless, they don’t understand you. They can’t give you what I can give you: a place to party, to meet your friends, to sleep in peace, without anyone talking to you about religion. Me, I give you the chance to make money,” he offers as an example.
« Nous sommes en compétition avec cette: “We’re competing with that outside offer. If we have nothing to offer them, it’s normal that they turn to those who offer them something concrete,” adds Pierreson Vaval.
Sa solution ? Écouter réellement les jeu: His solution? Truly listen to young people, “because often,” he continues, “we ask them questions, but they can tell we’re not ready to hear their answers. So they say what their parents want to hear. But if that openness doesn’t exist at home, they’ll go and express themselves elsewhere. We have to ask them what they’d like to change, show them that their thoughts matter to us.”
<strong>« Le dialogue, c’est d’abord une: “Dialogue is first and foremost about being present, being available”
Kahina Bouchefa, qui est assise à la gau: Kahina Bouchefa, who is seated to Pierreson Vaval’s left, nods. She agrees. “Dialogue is first and foremost about being present, being available. You have to find the balance between talking and leaving your child their privacy.”
« Il n’y a pas d’intervention miracle ;: “There’s no miracle intervention; it’s work that happens upstream. You have to pay attention to changes, to signs. It’s regular work of observing, of empathy. Changes in behaviour, even subtle ones, are often signs you shouldn’t ignore,” the psychologist insists.
Abdellah, connu du public commeAzzouz, p: Abdellah, known to the public as Azzouz, takes his turn to speak: “And there are signs that show a child is gradually changing. For example: a young person who drifts away, without explanation, from the friends they grew up with. Ask them why. They may not tell you right away that they have new friends or that they’ve started smoking, but those are clues you have to dig into. That’s already a sign to take seriously. Otherwise, in five or six months, you’ll see more serious changes: they start coveting expensive things because they’ve already made money illegally. The signs are there, but you have to be available to notice them.”
Abdellah met en lumière les difficultés: Abdellah highlights the difficulties faced by immigrant parents, who are more affected by poverty and therefore less available to their children: “These parents work hard to pay the bills and raise their children, but often they forget themselves… and forget their children. Many aren’t doing well psychologically. They want their children to succeed, but when you dig, you realize that success is often limited to school, as long as the child doesn’t bother them,” he says. “Yet success isn’t only academic. It’s also social, emotional. Does this child have dreams, ideas? Even with the sport the parents sign them up for, have we asked ourselves whether the child is really happy?”

<strong>Respecter nos jeunes, « leur mon: Respecting our youth, “showing them that they matter”
Hassan, père de trois enfants, prend la: Hassan, father of three, speaks with an amused smile. “I’ll give a thumbs up to what Abdellah is saying,” he jokes, drawing a few laughs. “Me, I wanted to get my kids into the culture here at all costs. I bought all the ski gear, but guess what? It was all for nothing. They hate skiing!” he says with a little burst of laughter. In a more serious tone, he continues: “So we tried something else: basketball, swimming, judo… And in the end, they chose judo. Today, they’re Canadian champions. I didn’t choose. I respected what they wanted, I supported them.” Hassan straightens in his seat: “If it had been up to me, I would have preferred soccer. But that’s what respect is. Respecting their choices and, more broadly, respecting their opinions, their questions. Quite simply, showing them that they matter.”
La conversation gagne en intensité lorsq: The conversation gains intensity when Abdellah opens a new front: “One problem I often notice is that parents tend to see their children as naive, whether they’re involved in organized crime or they’re excellent students. There’s a problem there… Do parents also need help to react in a system they didn’t grow up in?”
La psychologue Kahina Bouchefa enchaîne: Psychologist Kahina Bouchefa follows up immediately: “Indeed, it’s an interesting question to ask why these children are so influenced by what comes from outside. Without wanting to lecture parents, it’s clear that they need help, especially immigrant parents who don’t always have the codes and the keys to understand what’s going on around them.”
Selon la psychologue, l’écart entre les: According to the psychologist, the gap between the values parents instill in their children and those offered by the host society prevents good communication. “That fear that their children will accept the new values often leads them to avoid difficult discussions. Yet being a parent means accepting hearing what’s uncomfortable. It takes great strength, but also humility,” Kahina Bouchefa continues. “It’s not always denial, but rather an inability to build bridges between these worlds.”
Pierreson Vaval intervient à son tour. «: Pierreson Vaval steps in again. “No child is safe from violence. What makes the difference is what we give them at home.” He recounts that, when he was younger, he met gang recruiters on a basketball court. “When they came up to me and offered me a spot in their gang, I asked them if it would let me play more basketball. They said no, so I told them I wasn’t interested.” A few laughs are heard in the room. He continues, more seriously: “Know their dreams, support them, be partners in their happiness (...) [but] we can’t control everything,” he adds. “Some things depend on you, the parents; other things depend on the young person’s environment.”
Kahina Bouchefa reconnaît que beaucoup d: Kahina Bouchefa acknowledges that many parents don’t have all the tools to understand today’s world. “And that’s normal. They need support, just as they have to support their children.”
Des ressources, méconnues d’un grand nom: Resources that many parents don’t know about are nonetheless available, and within their own community, says Hassan. “If a parent doesn’t want an old-stock Québécois youth worker, there are North African ones. If parents prefer imams, there are some of those too,” he insists.
« Parfois, il suffit de signaler un prob: “Sometimes, all it takes is flagging a problem to open the door to help like food banks, legal clinics or sports programs,” continues youth worker Abdellah Azzouz. “A simple call to a community centre can make all the difference in steering a young person toward a positive environment,” he concludes.
Mais que faire lorsque la prévention ne: But what can be done when prevention is no longer enough and a young person is already involved in crime? Who can parents trust? Some refuse to turn to government services, which they consider far too punitive, out of fear of seeing their teenagers taken from their families. As for social workers, do they have the means needed to truly help these young people who are already caught in a spiral that is hard to break?
C’est une question sur laquelle s’attard: It’s a question La Converse will take up in an upcoming instalment of the “Our Neighbourhoods, Our Voices” article series.
